segments.text: AI is taking the world by storm.
It has superpowers that set it apart from any other software.
The reason is simple.
AI is built on a completely different foundation.
To see how different it is,
consider how normal software is created.
A programmer sits down and writes code line by line,
creating a core set of rigid instructions called rules.
This flowchart shows an if-then-else statement,
like a login screen.
A user enters a password.
If the password matches, then it opens the app.
Else, it shows an error message.
Because this path is fixed, it never changes.
Written rules return the same result every time.
AI does not use a programmer's written rules for every situation.
Instead, it relies entirely on patterns it learned during its development.
This board breaks down the two phases behind every AI answer.
First is the training phase.
The model learns from enormous amounts of data,
turning countless examples into learned numerical patterns before you ever use it.
Once trained, it answers one word at a time.
It uses probability to score how likely each possible next word is based on the word so far.
Then it chooses a likely next word, adds it, and repeats the process.
Learn patterns first, use them to build every answer.
To visualize this, think of normal software as a robot following a recipe in a cookbook.
Someone wrote every step, and the robot follows the rules to make the exact same dish every time.
AI is like a chef.
No one handed it a cookbook.
It cooked thousands of dishes, recognized the patterns of flavor and heat,
and can now cook a completely novel dish it has never made before.
This graphic shows that difference in action.
If you ask normal software, what's the best game for my new PS5?
The programmed rule checks a preset list and outputs the top entry.
It repeats Marvel Spider-Man 2 every single time you ask.
Ask AI software that exact same prompt, and it builds a fresh response word-by-word using learned patterns.
You might get NHL 26 the second time, and God of War Ragnarok the third.
Rules repeat the programmed answer.
Patterns build a fresh one.
If you want to calculate your GPA in a spreadsheet, you enter your grades and credits neatly into rows and columns.
That is structured data.
AI doesn't need this neatness.
It can process messy, real-world information, like details scribbled on the back of a receipt or buried in a copied text message.
That is unstructured data.
This lesson started as a series of handwritten notes on a legal pad, with lines crossed out and ideas moved around.
And AI was able to recognize the patterns in those messy notes and organize them into a clean first draft.
This diagram compares how both systems handle data.
Normal software forces you to fit information into an expected structure,
relying entirely on specific fields, file types, and commands it was built to handle.
AI software can look at those messy notes, PDFs, or audio files,
make sense of the chaos and transform it into a summary or a clean first draft.
While the available inputs and outputs depend on the app, the flexibility remains.
Normal software still wins for exact, consistent jobs like GPA math,
but AI earns its place on the open-ended messy jobs that defy rigid rules.
You bring the mess, and AI helps make sense of it.
A human can hold Kryptonite safely in a backpack, but for Superman, it can be fatal.
AI's unique superpowers come with their own specific Kryptonite.
Because AI runs on patterns instead of rules, trained behavior is harder to predict, inspect, and lock down.
This board highlights the real-world risks of unpredictability.
People use pattern building to generate scams that scale, creating fake identities and convincing messages in seconds.
There is also the issue of deep fakes.
The system can use its patterns to create convincing fake media that can be used to target or humiliate individuals.
Even without malicious intent, AI can hallucinate.
It can sound highly confident delivering medical or safety answers that are flat wrong.
The industry tries to manage these risks.
During training, they teach AI to avoid harmful behavior.
They also add a safety layer to the apps.
Guard rails designed to block or redirect harmful requests.
But these safety measures are imperfect.
They can accidentally block harmless requests or mis-dangerous ones.
This graphic sums up the trade-off.
AI's foundation gives it new superpowers.
Those superpowers come with Kryptonite.
